Running a One-Person Company: Finance, Tax, Equity & Cash Flow

2026 · 此间创, in conversation with Yang Jingjing

此间创 · Interview Companies, like people, run on money — and cash flow is the lifeline

In a wide-ranging 此间创 conversation, senior tax & financial consultant Yang Jingjing (杨静静) — a former university teacher who has advised 100+ companies — walks solo founders through the real backend of running a one-person company: registered capital, keeping company money apart from your own, partnership equity, and the cash flow that decides who survives.

The #1 trap for a one-person company, Yang says, is treating company money as personal money. A one-person limited company is still its own legal entity, and its limited-liability protection depends on one thing: keeping company assets clearly separate from personal assets (公私财产混同 is the risk). Pay per diems as expenses, take capital as loans, pay yourself a salary, and distribute profits only through proper procedures — every transaction needs a real business reason and proper documentation.

On bookkeeping, she warns against chasing the cheapest agent. Bookkeeping on its own is back-office record-keeping; a low-cost firm records your receipts by category without understanding what your company actually does, so the books balance but no longer reflect the real business. State tax authorities recognize real business — when the books and operations diverge, fines can run into tens of thousands of RMB, far more than the few hundred you saved.

Registered capital gets the same no-nonsense treatment. Under the new Company Law (from July 2024), limited companies must fully contribute their registered capital within five years, so the number is no longer just a badge of face. Set it against your actual operating costs and business scale, and remember that a bigger number is also a bigger shareholder liability you'll have to be able to honor.

On partnerships, she is blunt: decide who decides, on day one. Equity split is only step one; the decision mechanism matters more. Two partners should avoid 50/50 (aim for 51/49 or clearer), and four partners should never default to 25% each. Name who operates, who holds final decision power, how profits split, what happens if someone exits, whether shares can transfer, and any right of first refusal — before the honeymoon ends.

Two topics close the interview. Legally taking company money home means choosing the right path: salary (a personal-income-tax bracket of 3%–45%), a year-end bonus (eligible for separate taxation through end of 2027), or dividends (after value-added and corporate income taxes, 20% personal income tax on distributed profit — 80 of every 100 RMB). And finally, cash flow: the balance sheet is a company's foundation, the income statement its face, and the cash-flow statement its day-to-day. Yang has seen plenty of "profitable bankruptcies" — companies whose reports show profit while the bank account silently empties. Keep seven days to three months of cash reserve, watch accounts receivable, and never spend prepayments as if they were already earned profit.

Her parting idea frames the service industry's role as a "family doctor": catching problems before they explode, because prevention always costs less than the cure. It's a philosophy the Moon Bay Overseas Talent OPC community shares — building the backend support (registration, office, policy, finance, tax, HR, legal and resources) so solo founders can spend their energy on the product, not on the paperwork.
